# Manual implementation workspace template

A self-contained template for agent-managed workspaces in which **the user implements the work** while the agent plans, coaches, reviews and maintains the records.

Other templates in the family: `AGENTIC_LEARNING_WORKSPACE_TEMPLATE.md` (the agent implements step by step while the user builds along and learns), `AUTONOMOUS_AGENTIC_WORKSPACE_TEMPLATE.md` (agents build end to end; the user approves at milestone gates) and `ITERATIVE_HYBRID_WORKSPACE_TEMPLATE.md` (human-first with agent acceleration; the direction evolves and plans are written just in time).

## How to use this template

Provide this file to the agent (from the canonical repository or a local copy), together with the add-ons the project uses (see *Optional add-ons*), and supply the requirements separately. For example:

> Read MANUAL_IMPLEMENTATION_WORKSPACE_TEMPLATE.md and use it to generate or adapt this workspace's documentation and AGENTS.md. Use the requirements I provide separately. Preserve existing work and create only the first detailed plan for each active project. This request is for documentation, not implementation.

The example invocation does not need to be stored in generated documentation.

## Template use and updates

- The template is not retained in generated workspaces by default; a provenance note pointing to the canonical source is enough. Keep a retained copy only if the user asks for one. A template is not an automatically active `AGENTS.md` and is never copied verbatim into one.
- Generated workspaces record the canonical template file and the add-ons used as references in `docs/MEMORY.md` and in the generated `AGENTS.md`, once each, never as a local copy. If a recorded path is missing, ask the user for the updated path instead of guessing.
- When a workspace format or process change is agreed during a project, propose the matching template update so other workspaces inherit it. The templates are generated: edits go to the parts in the template repository's `src/` folder (`src/shared/` for rules every template uses, the template's own folder otherwise), then `scripts/build-templates.ps1` rebuilds them.
- The agent applies the process to the actual workspace, following the applicable instruction hierarchy and the user's current directions. The user can override the workflow and role defaults at any time. Preserve already-authorized scope instead of asking for the same permission again.

## Shared working rules

The working agreement states the working role; these rules hold alongside it.

- Records (`ROADMAP.md` states, `MEMORY.md` history, decisions, conventions, the skill ledger) and their compaction are agent-maintained; the user can inspect them at any time.
- Keep guidance concise: answer status check-ins ("what's next", "current status") with the current position and next action as pointers; keep steps and values in the plan and repeat them only when asked.
- Git, tool installs, publishing and external communication are user-managed unless explicitly delegated or requested; record a delegation and its boundaries in `MEMORY.md` conventions and `AGENTS.md`. Once source control is set up, individual commit/push operations are not tracked in the records; check the repository state directly when needed.
- Irreversible, destructive, costly or externally visible actions require explicit authorization for that action.
- Preserve existing work; do not reset, clean, move or overwrite unrelated material.
- No sub-agents unless the user or applicable instructions explicitly request them.
- The user can stop and resume at any point: the records must stand alone.

## Working agreement

- **The user implements.** The agent plans, explains concepts when first needed, reviews work, performs authorized verification and maintains the records, including the skill ledger.
- Creating or rewriting project code, assets, levels or configuration requires an explicit user request; documentation and non-destructive checks are normal agent work.
- Explain unfamiliar domain and tool concepts at first use and adapt to the user's stated knowledge; do not repeat generic lessons the user's background covers.
- Reviews give finding, location, consequence, suggested correction and a way to verify. The user applies corrections unless the agent has been asked to edit.

## Bootstrap procedure

1. Inspect existing instructions, files, documentation, implementation and repository state; identify what exists before proposing a structure.
2. Determine whether this is one project or a workspace of independently managed projects; use existing organization and user intent.
3. Extract confirmed requirements from the supplied material; keep proposals, assumptions, open questions and observed facts distinct.
4. Calibrate (see *Bootstrap additions*). Default user profile when nothing else is supplied: comfortable with general programming; no experience with this project's tools, frameworks, engine or conventions. Explain those at first use and skip generic programming lessons. Record only knowledge the user states for this workspace; do not carry it over from elsewhere or invent preferences.
5. Verify what the agent can verify itself (environment, installed tools, filesystem) before authoring plans.
6. Resolve ordinary organizational choices from available context; ask only questions that materially affect scope, correctness or the immediate plan. If requirements are missing, request them without inventing a product or domain; neutral scaffolding may still be prepared.
7. Check which add-ons the project needs (see *Optional add-ons*). Use the ones provided; for a needed add-on that was not provided, name it and ask for it, or proceed without it and state what is missing.
8. Preserve useful existing documents; adapt or link them instead of duplicating conflicting versions.
9. Generate the minimum coherent set: `README.md`, `AGENTS.md`, `docs/ROADMAP.md`, `docs/MEMORY.md`, a domain document only when the project has one (several → `docs/design/` with an index), the first detailed plan, and the agent-client entry files the user's clients need (see *Resume routine, AGENTS.md and client entry files*). No session files, no separate status, conventions, decisions, references or verification documents.
10. Check consistency of links, states and evidence labels; finish with the audit and handoff (see *Final audit and handoff*).

Scaffolding produces documentation only. Do not create product files, install dependencies, contact external services or initialize source control unless that work is separately requested or already authorized.

## Bootstrap additions

- Calibration (bootstrap step 4): seed the `MEMORY.md` skill ledger from what the user supplied; unknown skills start at L1.
- Verification (bootstrap step 5) exists so plans carry only user actions.
- Handoff: report the entry point, current plan and next action.

## Workspace structure

Preserve established naming and layout when they already provide the same responsibilities; record intentional deviations in `MEMORY.md` conventions.

### Single project

```text
<workspace>/
  README.md                Entry point: purpose, layout, how the workspace works
  AGENTS.md                Agent operating rules, resume routine, role-specific protocol
  CLAUDE.md                Optional client entry file: a pointer to AGENTS.md
  docs/
    ROADMAP.md             Roadmap, plan states, resume pointer; gates and notes as needed
    MEMORY.md              Decisions, conventions, the skill ledger, references, history
    history/YYYY-MM.md     Optional: archived history moved out of MEMORY at compaction
    <domain>.md            Project-specific concept or design document(s), as needed
    design/                Optional, when there are several domain docs: README.md index + one doc per system
    concepts.md            Optional: glossary of the project's tool, framework and engine concepts
    tooling-notes.md       Optional: tool recipes and environment reference too long for MEMORY
    tooling/               Optional, when several tools need notes: one file per tool instead of tooling-notes.md
    implementation-plans/
      NN-<name>.md            One current detailed plan; completed plans remain as records
    refs/                  Optional reference library: captures, fetched sets (+ `_sources.md` provenance), generated diagrams
  <delivery-root>/         Implementation lives where the project needs it
```

### Multiple projects

Repeat the `docs/` set per project (for example under `projects/<id>/`), keep the workspace-level `README.md` and `AGENTS.md`, and add a small registry (`PROJECTS.md` or a roadmap section) with one row per project: path, purpose, activity state, current plan link. Enforce one current plan per project. IDs and records are project-scoped; cross-project references use a qualified form such as `<project-id>:plan-03`. Nested `AGENTS.md` files contain only additions, never a copy of the root guide.

### Document responsibilities

| Document | Owns | Keep out |
|---|---|---|
| README.md | Purpose, layout, how the workspace works, where to start; a pointer to `ROADMAP.md` for the current position | Progress state and history (they drift; `ROADMAP.md` owns them) |
| AGENTS.md | Working agreement, resume routine, planning rules, role-specific protocol, records maintenance | Roadmap, design, transcripts |
| Client entry files (`CLAUDE.md` …) | A pointer to `AGENTS.md`; client-only notes | A copy of `AGENTS.md` |
| ROADMAP.md | Ordered milestones, plan states, resume pointer, gates, provisional estimates | Detailed tasks for future milestones; history |
| MEMORY.md | Decisions, conventions, the skill ledger, references, recent history | A second competing roadmap; invented preferences; long tool recipes |
| History archive (optional) | Older history entries moved out of MEMORY at compaction, one file per month | Decisions or conventions (those stay in MEMORY) |
| Tooling notes (optional) | Tool recipes, API quirks, environment reference material, verified commands | Decisions, progress |
| Domain document(s) | Project-specific concept or design that plans refer to: the *what and why*; with several, a `design/README.md` index (one line per doc) | Progress claims; plan steps |
| Concept glossary (optional) | The project's tool, framework and engine concepts, each explained once and linked from plans; created when the first concept is explained | Progress; decisions; generic programming lessons |
| Current plan | User part first (target, tasks, send line), agent notes below the divider; see *Plan format* | Bookkeeping above the divider |
| Completed plan files | Record of what was planned and delivered | Rewritten history |

Add domain-specific documents only when the actual project needs them. Do not generate empty documents. Optional files omitted from the workspace must also be omitted from navigation links.

## Planning rules

- Maintain a broad roadmap and **one current plan**. Do not write future plans during bootstrap.
- Author the next plan only after the current one has passed review with evidence; the user confirms before it is authored.
- Verify what is verifiable before authoring (environment, filesystem, installed tools).
- A plan ends in an observable, reviewable result; its size fits the work and the user's pace.
- Split a milestone before authoring its plan when: acceptance depends on later milestones · independent systems share only a final proof · several risky unknowns need early checks · no reviewable result appears within each group of work · a first-contact slice (what the next plans immediately depend on) separates cleanly from a completion slice that can wait until those plans need it.
- Design decisions the user may not be able to judge (layout, composition, structure) are drafted by the agent into a spec built from the reference material and corrected by the user; build steps then link that spec so the user judges concrete options instead of inventing.
- Keep plan IDs stable; a split after authoring keeps the number with letter suffixes (`03a`, `03b`), and any divergence between run order and numeric order is stated explicitly (for example under the roadmap table). Completed plan files remain as records.
- Mark finished items ✅ as they complete; acceptance criteria stay `[ ]` until the plan is Verified, then mark `[x]`.
- Changes to acceptance criteria must be justified and recorded. Never narrow them silently.
- Keep future roadmap entries outcome-level; treat their internals as provisional.
- Label estimates as rough and provisional; never invent delivery dates or commitments.
- Fold the previous plan's recorded learnings into the next plan.

Plan-format rules for every plan (*Plan format* gives the full format):

- Plan content that describes or recreates something visual (a build step, an approach description, a record note) links the reference or generated diagram that shows it (relative path, for example `../refs/<topic>/…`) so the picture sits beside the text.
- The plan header line carries the state, a progress grid (`⬜`/`✅`), the next item and the roadmap link.
- Plans are agent-neutral: they name files, commands and outcomes, not client-specific tool names, so any supported agent client can execute them.
- Each fact has one home: design docs (what/why), plans (how/now), the glossary (concepts), `MEMORY.md` (decisions, history), `ROADMAP.md` (where we are). Other documents link to it (`../design/<doc>.md#<section>`) instead of repeating it.

## Plan format

```markdown
# Plan NN — [Short title]
`[Planned|Pending|In progress|Done|Verified]` · `⬜⬜⬜⬜⬜⬜⬜ n/N` · next → N · roadmap: ../ROADMAP.md

🎯 [Target — the observable result, one or two lines.]

### 1. [Action]
&emsp;&emsp;1.1 [Step]

&emsp;&emsp;1.2 [Step]

💡 [Colocated note — only where a new concept or a genuine trap sits.]

**Done when:** [what is true when this task is complete.]

### 2. [Action]
…

📤 When done: [the evidence only the user can provide.]

---
## 🔧 Agent notes
*Bookkeeping and review only — not implementation reading.*
- **Acceptance** (checked at review; marked when Verified): [criteria]
- **Known traps**: [short list]
- **Scope guard**: [what this plan deliberately does not include]
- **Environment** verified [date]: [facts the agent checked itself]
- **Inspect**: [files, configs, structure to check at review]
- **Limits**: [what cannot be verified from files]
- **Record**: [what to log at review — decisions, layout outcomes, ledger updates]
```

Format rules:

- The user part comes first and carries no bookkeeping; everything after the `---` divider is agent material and can be skipped by the user.
- The user part is target, tasks, send line. Plans contain only user actions.
- Tasks are numbered `1`, `2`, …; steps are numbered `1.1`, `1.2`, … under their task, each on its own line indented with `&emsp;&emsp;` (Markdown lists cannot express `1.1`).
- Mark a finished step ✅ leading its line, and a finished task by appending ✅ to its heading once its checkpoint passes.
- Tasks are actions. Use exact steps where the tooling is first-time (see *Support levels*); explanations are colocated at the step that needs them, never a separate study section before the steps.
- Each task closes with a `**Done when:**` statement; the aggregate acceptance list lives in the agent block.
- The send line asks only for evidence the agent cannot produce or inspect itself.
- Known traps and verified environment let the agent answer quickly and cold-start safely.

**Task anatomy**

- **Why (optional):** one line linking the task to the target, only when non-obvious.
- **Steps:** ordered, concrete actions. Exact editor paths, menu names and field values at L1; less hand-holding as the level drops.
- **Code:** task-scoped deltas only: file path, anchor, the lines to add, replace or delete, clearly marked. A complete file only when the task creates that small file. Explain only APIs the user has not met.
- **Done when:** what is true, visible or runnable when the task is complete; add an evidence hint where non-obvious.

## Support levels

Task detail adapts to demonstrated skill, not a fixed global setting:

| Level | Use when | Detail |
|---|---|---|
| L1 Guided | First occurrence of a skill | Exact steps and field values; code deltas with short per-line explanations; intermediate results stated. |
| L2 Supported | One clean repetition completed | Concrete steps and expected result; code described (signature, location, behavior); snippet on request or for a genuinely new API. |
| L3 Independent | Two clean repetitions completed | Goal, constraints and acceptance; snippets only for genuinely new APIs; the agent reviews the result. |

- Record the skill, evidence and current level in the `MEMORY.md` skill ledger. The recorded level drives task detail; task headings carry no level label.
- A clean repetition means the task was completed and its checkpoint passed without correction. If the user struggles or the task introduces a new API, teach that occurrence one level more detailed, then return to the recorded level after a clean repetition.
- For a first occurrence whose deliverable spans many similar units (zones, screens, systems), checkpoint after each unit (build it, look at it, short check) rather than only at the task's end.
- Levels are per skill; a plan may mix them. Adjust remaining task detail when checkpoint evidence warrants; record changes at review.
- Support levels change presentation detail only. Acceptance criteria and verification requirements never change with the level.

## Records, states and evidence

Plan states (the fourth state is described under *States*):

| State | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Planned | Roadmap entry only; plan not authored |
| Pending | Plan exists; approval or start pending |
| In progress | Implementation or correction is underway |
| Done | The user reports completion; review or required evidence remains |
| Verified | Review passed and applicable observable acceptance has evidence |

- `ROADMAP.md` owns the roadmap, plan states and the resume pointer. `MEMORY.md` owns decisions, conventions, the skill ledger, references and history; history entries are labeled `YYYY-MM-DD-NN` (workspace-wide sequence).
- After meaningful work: update `ROADMAP.md` (states, resume pointer) and `MEMORY.md` (history entry, decisions, learning or skill updates); keep them consistent. No session files.
- On the user's "compact": condense history (recent detailed → older one-liners); never silently remove decisions, evidence labels or learning and skill records. Correct errors by annotation, not silent rewriting.

**Record size budget.** The resume routine reads `ROADMAP.md` and `MEMORY.md` every session, so both must stay readable in one pass:

- `MEMORY.md` targets ≤ ~25 KB. History keeps the current plan's entries (at most ~5) detailed, each ≤ ~5 lines; older entries are one line each (label · what happened · outcome, with pointers to decisions or commits). When the file exceeds the budget, compact proactively and say so in the history entry; the compaction rules above still apply.
- Conventions are rules, one or two lines each. Tool recipes, API quirks, long environment inventories and engine or tool reference material go in the tooling notes (or the applicable add-on) with a one-line pointer in Conventions.
- Tooling notes list a command only after it has been run in the workspace, with the shell it runs in. When the project starts long-running processes (servers, containers, editors), they open with a **Check first** section: how to see what is already running, what "nothing running" looks like, and how to stop it, free a port or reset state.
- `ROADMAP.md`'s resume block is a few lines: position, current plan, next action, gate. No history; that lives in `MEMORY.md`.
- Long-running workspaces may move older one-line history into `docs/history/YYYY-MM.md` at compaction, leaving one pointer line per archived month in `MEMORY.md`. Archived entries are moved verbatim, never rewritten; decisions, conventions and evidence labels stay in `MEMORY.md`.
- Other documents have soft budgets so no file becomes the one large document: `AGENTS.md` ~10 KB (recipes move to tooling notes), `ROADMAP.md` ~10 KB (outcome-level only), each domain or design doc ~15 KB (split by system and update the index), each plan ~20 KB (split with letter suffixes, see *Planning rules*).

Evidence categories, kept separate:

1. **Inspection:** what was read or reviewed and what it supports.
2. **Executed checks:** commands or actions actually run, with context and observed results.
3. **User-reported checks:** what the user says they tested, clearly attributed.
4. **Not checked:** missing environments, omitted scenarios, unresolved findings.

Match the check to the claim: use the cheapest check that settles it (targeted inspection before full runs) and escalate only when the scenario requires it. Distinguish "configured correctly" from "actually works": values visible in a tool's UI are evidenced by user screenshots (user-reported), while heavier runtime or session checks are reserved for claims configuration alone cannot settle (constructed state, runtime wiring, integration, feel). Binary or non-text artifacts need suitable evidence; filenames alone are insufficient. Never equate generated files with working behavior, or a planned check with an executed one.

Visual defects (rendering artifacts, misplaced or missing elements): reproduce before fixing, isolate by toggling the suspect element at runtime, and close only on an executed before/after capture where the tooling allows; "it went away" after an unrelated change is not a closure. Parity checks against a reference (template, earlier version) diff the full property set, not a hand-picked list.

**Verification levels** (optional; recommended once checks can be automated; each task then names one). The project's tooling notes give the exact commands; engine add-ons give recipes (for Unreal: `UNREAL_TEST_AUTOMATION.md`).

| Level | When | Typical content | Budget |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Fast** | Every change | Build, static and data validation, lint and format checks, unit tests, headless | minutes |
| **Standard** | Every task (default) | Fast plus functional or integration tests of the behavior, including networked or multi-process checks where the behavior spans processes | ≤ ~15 min |
| **Full** | Plan end where acceptance needs it; milestone gates and demos | Standard plus multi-client or integration runs, performance budgets, visual captures compared with references, packaging; then the user's manual check | ~1 h + user time |

Evidence lines record the level, command, result and artifact path, using the evidence categories above. A planned check is never reported as an executed one.

## States and review protocol

Plans: Planned → Pending → In progress → **Done** (the user reports completion; review or required evidence remains) → **Verified**.

Standard review protocol: the user provides run evidence (short clip or screenshots, what was tested, versions); the agent inspects project files, configuration and structure where the domain allows, and reviews user-provided evidence of behavior. Binary or non-text artifacts (compiled assets, graphs, levels) need suitable user evidence.

Record review findings with a stable identifier when follow-up requires it:

```markdown
| Finding | Severity / consequence | Location | Suggested correction | Verification | State |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
```

## Decisions, conventions and sources

All three live in `MEMORY.md`.

- **Decisions:** stable IDs scoped to the workspace or project; states Confirmed, Proposed, Deferred, Superseded. One line each: decision, basis, rejected alternatives (a few words on why each lost), revisit trigger, and a pointer to where the full reasoning sits (plan section or history entry). Never silently rewritten; a superseded decision names its successor. Ratify Proposed decisions once the work they govern is underway. The basis lives in the repository (a history entry or a file in the workspace), not only in an external file.
- **Tried and dropped:** an approach abandoned during the work is recorded where it happened (the plan's agent notes or a history entry): what was tried, the evidence that ruled it out, what replaced it. A dead end that shaped a decision is also listed among that decision's rejected alternatives.
- **Conventions:** paths, IDs, naming, markers, evidence labels, repository rules (for example which build artifacts to ignore, and an explicit ignore or attribute decision when a new artifact class first appears), compaction rules, supported agent clients. Fetched third-party material keeps a provenance note beside it (source, date, usage) and stays reference-only.
- **References:** checked sources with dates and versions; unchecked items labeled as to-verify. Research prefers official or primary sources; documentation about a tool is not evidence that the local environment was tested.

## Resume routine, AGENTS.md and client entry files

Resume routine: `docs/ROADMAP.md` (roadmap, states, resume pointer) → `docs/MEMORY.md` (decisions, conventions, the skill ledger, recent history) → the current detailed plan → domain documents when design context matters → tooling notes when tool work is next. State the next action as a plan pointer and continue from the recorded position; do not restart planning.

The generated `AGENTS.md` includes, beyond the items in *AGENTS.md additions*:

1. The working agreement and how the user changes it.
2. The exact resume reading order with paths that exist in this workspace, domain documents named.
3. Planning rules: one current plan, on-demand authoring, verify-before-authoring, review gate before the next plan.
4. Authorization boundaries for risky, external or costly actions; repository delegation if any.
5. Records maintenance, compaction rules and the record size budget.
6. The plan markers legend.
7. Implementation and documentation roots, repository conventions.
8. The user profile: the default (see *Bootstrap procedure*) plus knowledge and preferences actually supplied.
9. The canonical template file and the add-ons used, as references only; the rule to ask the user when a path is missing; the rule to propose template updates when formats change.

Do not copy the template into `AGENTS.md`. Do not insert a technology stack, fixed milestone count, domain-specific verification matrix or experience profile unless the user's requirements justify it.

**Client entry files.** `AGENTS.md` is the single source of agent rules. A client that does not read `AGENTS.md` natively gets a thin entry file that points to it, never a copy. For Claude Code: a root `CLAUDE.md` whose content is `@AGENTS.md` (the import loads the file), plus client-only notes when there are any. Create entry files only for clients the user actually uses, and record the supported clients in `MEMORY.md` conventions. Tool-server (MCP) configuration is per client and per project (for example OpenCode `opencode.json`, Claude Code `.mcp.json`); when more than one client is supported, keep their entries equivalent. The add-ons give the shapes.

## AGENTS.md additions

The generated `AGENTS.md` also includes:

1. How authorized implementation requests change the working agreement.
2. Coaching: support levels, ledger location, how detail adapts.
3. The review protocol and evidence categories.
4. The plan markers legend: states Planned → Pending → In progress → Done → Verified; `🎯 💡 ✅ ⬜ 📤 🔧`; `**Done when:**` checkpoints.

## Final audit and handoff

Before reporting the workspace ready, check (plus *Audit additions*):

- All supplied requirements are captured without adding unrequested scope; proposals, observations and open questions are distinguishable.
- Single-project versus multi-project structure is coherent and documented.
- Every active project has at most one current plan; completed plans remain intact; future milestones stay outcome-level.
- Completed items are ✅; acceptance is `[x]` only for Verified plans; states agree with `ROADMAP.md`.
- Records live only in `ROADMAP.md` and `MEMORY.md` (plus optional tooling notes and history archive); no stray status, session or duplicate documents; records and documents are within their size budgets.
- The README holds no progress state; the roadmap's resume block is current.
- The environment the agent can verify was verified before authoring plans.
- Links resolve, tables and fences are valid, and actionable documents have no unresolved boilerplate.
- Evidence labels are honest: only checks actually performed; missing evidence is identified.
- Decisions carry their rejected alternatives and a pointer to the full reasoning; dead ends are recorded where they happened.
- The generated `AGENTS.md` is concise, uses correct paths and agrees with the working role; client entry files point to it.
- Needed add-ons are in use or their absence is recorded.
- The next action is concrete and feasible, or the exact missing prerequisite is identified.

Finish with links to the workspace entry point, roadmap and current plan; state what was created or adapted, what was verified and what remains pending. Do not claim the deliverable is implemented or verified because its documentation has been generated.

## Audit additions

- The current plan is one coherent slice; the next plan is gated on review plus user confirmation.
- Plans follow the format: target, tasks, send line, agent notes below the divider; explanations are colocated, not study sections; plans contain only user actions.
- Task detail matches the recorded support levels; headings carry no level label; acceptance criteria are unchanged by level.

## Optional add-ons

Add-ons are separate files in the template repository for specific tooling. They supplement this template and never change its working agreement. Use one when the project involves its area; record the ones used in `MEMORY.md` references.

| Add-on | Use when | If needed but not provided |
|---|---|---|
| `UNREAL_MCP_BRIDGE.md` | An Unreal Engine project where the agent should inspect or edit the editor (MCP bridges, reference-material pipeline) | Ask for it; without it, editor work becomes user steps with screenshot evidence |
| `UNREAL_TEST_AUTOMATION.md` | An Unreal Engine project with automated checks (builds, automation and functional tests, captures, packaging per verification level) | Ask for it; without it, define the commands in the tooling notes as they are verified |
| `BLENDER_MCP_BRIDGE.md` | Blender scene work or batch asset pipelines, Unreal export conventions | Ask for it; without it, Blender work becomes user steps |
| `ASSET_GENERATION_PIPELINE.md` | 3D assets or concept and reference images are sourced or generated (packs, AI 3D, Blender; provenance and licences) | Ask for it; without it, record sources and licences by hand |
| `AGENT_ORCHESTRATION.md` | The autonomous template with a cheaper worker client (dispatch, report format, dry run) | The orchestrator implements the cards itself |

Helper scripts used by the add-ons live in the template repository's `scripts/` folder.
